name: Golden Roof
label: Golden Roof
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Herzog-Friedrich-Straße' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Herzog-Friedrich-Straße nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/103128011: the OpenStreetMap point 'Golden Roof Museum'.
notes: Famous gilded balcony in the old town.

text.description:
The Golden Roof is the balcony-and-roof feature on the front of a late-medieval building in Innsbruck's Old Town, and the city's best-known symbol. It was finished in 1500 for Emperor Maximilian I, who wanted a private box from which he and his wife, Bianca Maria Sforza, could watch festivals and tournaments in the square below. The roof carries about 2,657 fire-gilded copper tiles (other counts give 2,738). The carved reliefs and painted panels you see today are careful replicas, and the originals are kept in the Ferdinandeum museum.

It photographs well because the gilded roof stands out against the soft pastel facades of the street. This is the classic postcard view. The street is narrow, so the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps you fit in the whole scene. For a tighter shot, step back a little and use the default lens (1x). Use a zoom lens for the carved reliefs and coats of arms on the balcony.

The street is a pedestrian zone and gets very busy around midday, so early morning or late afternoon is calmer and kinder to the light. For a second angle, try the view that fits the richly decorated Helblinghaus into the same frame as the Golden Roof.
text.geographic_location: The Golden Roof is in Innsbruck's Old Town (Altstadt), on the square at the heart of the historic centre.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town (Altstadt) in the centre of Innsbruck and look for Herzog-Friedrich-Straße. From there the roof is about 16 m ahead, to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in the whole street, the roof and the mountains. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße (mid-street, facing the Golden Roof). The Golden Roof centred in a frontal view, framed by pastel Old Town facades with the Nordkette mountains rising behind the rooftops. From here the roof sits in the centre of the frame, with pastel Old Town facades on either side and the Nordkette mountains rising behind the rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the Golden Roof on the centre line, keeping the phone level so the facades don't lean inwards. Include the colourful buildings on both sides and a strip of mountain above the rooftops. For a variation, try the view from the Helblinghaus side, which puts its decorated facade and the roof in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the golden roof to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the gilding keeps its detail and the sky doesn't turn white. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames, so you can pick one without passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, to avoid harsh overhead midday sun and the busiest crowds.

text.access_note: The outside of the Golden Roof can be photographed from the open pedestrian street at any time, but the balcony can only be seen from inside the museum, so check the official site before you go.

name: Nordkette
label: Nordkette Mountains
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Marktplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Marktplatz' (way/91910602): middle (129 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM N2028102837 (Nordkette): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Mountain wall above the city, best viewed from the old town.

text.description: The Nordkette is the steep ridge that rises straight up behind Innsbruck, and it is what makes the city look so dramatic in photos. The classic frame is not of the mountain alone. Look across the Inn from Marktplatz and you see the colourful row of Mariahilf houses along the water, with the rocky ridge standing behind them. Several guides treat this as Innsbruck's classic city-and-mountain shot, and guides call this the best vantage point for the coloured houses against the mountains. The houses sit in the foreground, so the mountain is partly behind them rather than fully open. That is what gives the picture its layers: water, bright façades, then rock. The view depends on the weather, and guides say the peaks are often hidden in cloud, so check the forecast before you go. If the top is cloudy, the houses and river still make a pleasant photo, but the mountain will not be the star. For a different take, Maria-Theresien-Straße runs straight towards the ridge with the Annasäule column in the middle of the frame. Bergisel, the ski-jump hill, shows the Nordkette's sheer rock wall framing the city from the south. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the ridge looks quite different when it is closer.
text.geographic_location: The Nordkette is the mountain ridge on the north side of Innsbruck, rising above the city. The viewpoint is Marktplatz, a square a short walk from the Golden Roof, looking across the Inn.
text.directions_text: Start from the Golden Roof, from where Marktplatz is a short walk. Once at Marktplatz, face north across the Inn towards the Mariahilf houses; the Nordkette is the ridge behind them. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the houses, the river and the ridge in one frame. If the ridge looks small, try telephoto (2x-3x) to bring the mountain closer and make it feel bigger behind the houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Marktplatz (Looking across the Inn toward the Mariahilf houses, with the Nordkette behind them). The colourful Mariahilf row of houses on the Inn in the foreground, with the steep Nordkette ridge rising behind. The photo shows the colourful row of houses on the river in the foreground, with the steep Nordkette ridge rising behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the line of houses on the lower third, so the ridge fills the upper part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the houses do not lean. If you want a different view, Maria-Theresien-Straße gives a long street leading to the ridge with the Annasäule in the middle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the ridge to focus and set the exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. Wait for a gap in the cloud if the top is hidden.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun is behind you and lights the houses (one guide says so). Check the forecast first, as the peaks are often in cloud.

text.access_note: Marktplatz is an open public square; the cable cars up the mountain and the Bergisel ski-jump tower are separate and may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ambras Castle
label: Ambras Castle
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Unterschloss' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Unterschloss' (way/44221565): middle (101 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1432849: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Schloss Ambras' (71 m across).
notes: Renaissance castle on the southeastern edge of the city.

text.description:
Ambras Castle is a Renaissance castle in the hills above Innsbruck, sitting at 632 metres above sea level. It was built in the 16th century on the site of an earlier castle from the 10th century. Archduke Ferdinand II had it rebuilt as a gift for his wife, Philippine Welser. He also filled it with his collections, and the Lower Castle was built specially to house them. That makes it one of the oldest museums in the world.

The best photo here is taken from Unterschloss, the lower castle courtyard inside the grounds. The old buildings, arcades and formal gardens frame the castle's Renaissance architecture and give the picture plenty of depth. One guide recommends midday light for this courtyard.

If you have time for a second picture, the Belvedere shows Innsbruck and the mountains behind the castle grounds, with the castle in frame at sunset. The approach drive on Schlossstraße is a third option for the castle's exterior.

Keep your phone steady with both hands and use the gridlines to keep the arcades straight. Walk around the courtyard rather than shooting everything from one spot, because each corner gives a different mix of arches, walls and garden.
text.geographic_location: Ambras Castle stands on a hillside in the hills above Innsbruck. The lower courtyard, Unterschloss, is inside the castle grounds.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to Schloss Ambras. Guides describe Schlossstraße as the approach drive to the castle. From there, the Unterschloss courtyard inside the grounds is the place to take the castle photo. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the courtyard and castle together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the courtyard feels tight and you want the arcades and gardens in frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (the lower castle courtyard, inside the grounds). The lower courtyard with its historic buildings, arcades and formal gardens, framing the castle's Renaissance architecture. The recommended viewpoint is Unterschloss, the lower castle courtyard inside the grounds. From there you see the lower courtyard with its historic buildings, arcades and formal gardens, which frame the castle's Renaissance architecture.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up an arcade or a building edge with a vertical line so the walls stay straight. Include a strip of garden in the foreground to add depth. If you want a wider view with the mountains, the Belvedere is an alternative viewpoint, and it works well at sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or sunlit stone looks too bright. Hold the phone still for a moment before pressing the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Midday, according to one guide. For the wider view from the Belvedere, go at sunset.

text.access_note: Ambras Castle is a museum with grounds and may be ticketed or have seasonal restrictions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bergisel Ski Jump
label: Bergisel Ski Jump
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1016830386: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bergisel Schanze' (384 m across).
notes: Zaha Hadid ski jump with a panoramic view of the city.

text.description: The Bergisel Ski Jump is one of Innsbruck's best-known sporting landmarks, and its sweeping modern lines make it a rewarding subject for a phone. The jump has a stadium with room for 26,000 people. It is a regular stop on the ski jumping World Cup calendar and hosts the third competition of the Four Hills Tournament every year. The site has a long history. The first competitions here in the 1920s used simple wooden constructions, and a larger hill was built in 1930. It was rebuilt before the 1964 Winter Olympics and used again for the 1976 Games. The hill you see today was finished in 2003 and designed by the architect Zaha Hadid. That mix of sport history and contemporary design is what makes it interesting to photograph. The long, tapering profile of the jump works well as a strong diagonal line, and the stadium bowl below gives a sense of scale. For a good photo, step back far enough to take in the whole shape, and look for people or small details in the foreground to show how big it is. Take a few shots from different distances, since the jump looks quite different close up and from further away. Stay on public paths and areas you are allowed in, and follow any signs or staff instructions.
text.geographic_location: The jump is in the Bergisel area of Innsbruck, Austria.
text.directions_text: Start from central Innsbruck and head to Bergisel. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or ask locally for the Bergisel Ski Jump (Bergiselschanze). Once you are in the area, the phone icon on the map is at the jump itself. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole jump in, then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the structure.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. That means the structure is all around you, so step back as far as you safely and legally can to get its full shape in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use the long diagonal of the jump as the main line of the picture. Keep the camera level so the vertical parts do not lean. Include a person or railing in the foreground for scale. Then take a closer shot of one detail with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the jump to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so it does not wash out. Hold the phone with both hands, since the wide lens exaggerates any tilt.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a structure like this, and a clear day gives you a clean sky behind it. On competition days it will be busier, so allow extra time.

text.access_note: Check the official site for access details before you go.

name: Hofburg, Innsbruck
label: Imperial Palace
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/312708485: the OpenStreetMap point 'Hofburg'.

text.description: The Hofburg is the former Habsburg palace on the eastern edge of Innsbruck's old town, and it is a good subject for a phone photo. Its long, calm Baroque front gives you clean lines and soft colours, and the older parts of the building show up as small details along the way. The first palace was built around 1460 under Archduke Sigismund. It later grew into a large complex that also takes in the Hofkirche, the cathedral and the Court Garden. The main façade on the Rennweg dates from 1766 to 1773, in the time of Empress Maria Theresa. If you look closely, you can still see older pieces worked into the building. One example is the Heraldic Tower, which was converted in 1499 from an earlier city gate. The palace stayed with the Habsburgs for more than 450 years, and today it holds museum rooms. For a good all-round shot, stand back far enough to fit the whole length of the façade into the frame, and keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. Then move closer and use a zoom setting to pick out a tower, a doorway or a window row. The phone icon on the map is a short step from the palace itself, so the building will fill much of your view. Traffic and passers-by may drift into the frame, so take a few shots and pick the cleanest one.
text.geographic_location: The Hofburg stands on the eastern edge of Innsbruck's old town, with its main front on the Rennweg. It sits next to the Hofgarten (Court Garden), the Hofkirche and the cathedral.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from the old town around the Goldenes Dachl, which lies west of the Hofburg, and head east towards the Rennweg. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Hofburg. Once you reach the Rennweg, look for the phone icon on the map, a few steps from the palace. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers, windows and other details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You are very close, so the palace will fill most of the frame at 1x.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edge of the façade with a vertical grid line so the walls do not lean. Take one wide shot of the full front, then a closer one of a tower or doorway. Wait for a gap in the traffic and pedestrians before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the façade colours stay rich. Hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the façade has more shape. Early in the day usually means fewer people in the frame too.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the street, but the museum rooms inside are a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for access and any ticket rules.

name: Court Church
label: Court Church
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/48364648: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Court Church' (66 m across).
notes: Holds Maximilian I's tomb with the Black Men statues.

text.description:
The Court Church (Hofkirche) is a Gothic church in Innsbruck's Old Town, built in 1553 by Emperor Ferdinand I as a memorial to his grandfather, Emperor Maximilian I. Maximilian is not actually buried here, so the grand black marble tomb in the middle of the nave is a cenotaph, an empty monument. Around it stand 28 large bronze figures of ancestors, relatives and heroes, each taller than a person. The church also holds the tomb of Andreas Hofer, Tyrol's national hero, and a Renaissance organ from 1560.

It photographs well because the subject is so varied. Outside you get a plain, steep-roofed building next to the Hofburg, with a finely carved Renaissance portal. Inside, the bronze statues surround the dark tomb, which makes strong shapes. On a phone the easiest pictures are the statues close up, the tomb's carved panels, and one wide shot of the nave.

Churches are often dim inside, so be ready to hold the phone steadily and let the camera take its time. Move slowly between shots, because the statues stand around the tomb and the angle changes a lot with each step. Photography rules inside can differ from outside, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Court Church stands in the Altstadt (Old Town) of Innsbruck, at Universitätsstraße 2, right beside the Hofburg (the imperial palace).
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make your way to the Old Town (Altstadt) of Innsbruck and walk to the Hofburg, with the church right beside it at Universitätsstraße 2. The phone icon on the map is at the church itself, so there is no extra walk once you reach it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the outside of the church and for general views of the nave. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tomb and the surrounding statues in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single statues and the carved panels.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Outside, stand as close to the building as you like and shoot along the wall and up at the portal. If you go inside, the tomb is in the middle of the nave, so start from near the entrance and work around the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight so the church doesn't lean. Inside, line the nave up with the centre of the screen so the tomb and the surrounding statues are framed symmetrically. For a portrait of a single statue, step in close and let the dark background fall away.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the subject to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the bronze keeps its detail. If it is dim inside, let night mode work and hold the phone still against your body or a pillar until it finishes. Use portrait mode only for statues that stand clear of the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The outside is easiest to photograph in soft daylight, such as morning or late afternoon, and early or late in the day usually means fewer people in the way. Churches can be dim inside whatever the time, so choose the time that suits your visit and check the official opening arrangements first.

text.access_note: This is a church with a famous cenotaph, so entry arrangements and photography rules inside may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: Alpenzoo
label: Alpine Zoo
camera_source: Commons cluster (6 photos), weak. Moved 87 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 110 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/145107933: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Alpenzoo' (345 m across).

text.description:
Alpenzoo is a zoo on a mountain slope in Innsbruck, and it is one of the highest-elevation zoos in Europe. It was founded on 22 September 1962 by the zoologist Hans Psenner. It is home to about 2,000 animals from 150 species. Bears, wolves, moose and bison are the big draws, along with birds of prey, and it is the only zoo in the world that shows the wallcreeper. It also has a timber pavilion shaped like a snail, opened in August 2017, which makes a good shape to frame against the trees.

For a phone photographer the appeal is the mix of animals and a steep, wooded setting, with winding footpaths that give you changing angles as you climb. Look for a clear gap in the fencing, or stand close to the glass, and keep your lens as near the barrier as you can to cut out reflections. Take a few wide shots of the slope and the paths too, so your photos show the setting as well as the animals. Some paths are quite steep, so allow time and watch your footing while you hold your phone. Most areas are reachable by wheelchair, but not every path.
text.geographic_location: Alpenzoo sits on a mountain slope within the city of Innsbruck, in Tyrol, Austria. The Weiherburg café and restaurant is part of the grounds.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is given for this spot, so check a local route planner for the best way up from central Innsbruck. From there it is about 2 minutes on foot to the middle of the zoo, heading south-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of enclosures and paths. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the slope, the snail-shaped pavilion and views through the trees. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for animals further back, so you do not need to lean over barriers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (upper part of the zoo, at the top of the fox enclosure area). Panoramic view over the city of Innsbruck and the surrounding mountains, with Alpine animals in the foreground. From there you can photograph the wooded slope and the paths running across it, with the zoo spread out in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the animal or the pavilion on one of the grid intersections, leaving some trees or path around it to show the hillside setting. Get your lens close to the glass or through a gap in the mesh to avoid reflections and wire in the frame. Portrait mode can work for animals that are fairly close and still.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the animal's eye to focus, not on the mesh or glass, then slide the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright behind it. Try Live Photos for moving animals, and pick the sharpest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a bright but not harsh day, when shade under the trees is soft and the animals are more likely to be up and about. Check the official site for opening times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed zoo, so check the official site before you go for opening times and entry details.

name: St. Anne's Column
label: St. Anne's Column
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maria-Theresien-Straße' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Maria-Theresien-Straße and Meraner Straße (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/748361873: the OpenStreetMap point 'St. Anne's Column'.

text.description:
St. Anne's Column stands in the middle of Maria-Theresien-Straße, the pedestrian street through Innsbruck's city centre. It was put up to give thanks after the last Bavarian troops were driven out of the Tyrol on Saint Anne's Day (26 July) in 1703. It was consecrated in 1706. The column is red Kramsach marble, designed by the sculptor Cristoforo Benedetti, and rises 13 metres. On top is the Virgin as the Woman of the Apocalypse. Four saints stand around the base: Saint Anne to the north, Cassian to the west, Vigilius to the east and Saint George to the south.

The area photographs well because this is a busy pedestrian street with colourful, painted Baroque-style facades on both sides and mountains above the rooftops. The column is not the main subject from here. The picture is the colourful, detailed facades with the mountains rising behind them. The column itself is a short walk along the street to the north, where you can take a closer shot of the monument.

The street is busy, so be patient and keep clear of café seating. Please do not sit on the monument's steps, as café owners dislike it.
text.geographic_location: In Innsbruck's city centre, on the pedestrian street Maria-Theresien-Straße.
text.directions_text: Head for the Old Town and the pedestrian stretch of Maria-Theresien-Straße. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facades and the mountains above them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole junction in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftop and facade details. The column is better photographed from near it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Maria-Theresien-Straße and Meraner Straße (the building corner at the Meraner Straße intersection, a short walk from the column). Colourful Baroque-era facades at the street junction, with the mountains rising above the rooftops; the column itself is not the main subject. From here the photo shows the colourful Baroque-era facades at the junction, with the mountains rising above the rooftops. The column is further along the street to the north and is not the main subject.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a facade edge up with a vertical grid line, so the buildings do not lean. Keep the rooftop line in the lower half of the frame and give the mountains the upper part. If you want the column as the main subject, walk up to it and shoot looking north. The Nordkette mountains rise behind the Old Town, and you will see the Saint George statue on the south face of the base.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-toned facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the painted colours keep their detail. Use ultra-wide sparingly, as it can stretch people and buildings near the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on this busy street. When facing north, the sun is mostly behind you around midday, which tends to light the front of the buildings and the column.

text.access_note: This is an open public pedestrian street, but it is busy and sometimes used for events, so check the official site before you go if you are planning around a particular date.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the street is likely to be quieter.
Facing north around midday, the sun is mostly behind the photographer and lights the front of the buildings and the column.
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch people and buildings near the edges of the frame.

name: Triumphal Arch, Innsbruck
label: Triumphal Arch
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Maria-Theresien-Straße' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1237886555: the OpenStreetMap point 'Triumphpforte'.
notes: Arch at the south end of Maria-Theresien-Straße.

text.description:
The Triumphal Arch (Triumphpforte) stands at the southern end of Maria-Theresien-Straße, once the road out of the city to the south. It is one of Innsbruck's best-known sights, and it works well on a phone because it is a solid, symmetrical shape that is easy to frame. In good weather, mountains may appear behind it; check on the day which one shows.

It was built in 1765 for the wedding of Archduke Leopold, son of Empress Maria Theresa, to the Spanish princess Maria Luisa. Leopold's father, Francis Stephen, died unexpectedly shortly after the wedding. A memorial theme was therefore added: the south side shows the wedding, and the north side remembers the emperor. Unusually for such an arch, it was built in stone rather than wood, reusing blocks from the old outer city gate.

For photos, aim to get the whole arch in one frame, with any mountains and buildings behind it. The phone icon on the map is at the arch itself. For a wider frame with the arch in front, you could try the central traffic island at the southern end of Maria-Theresien-Straße. Treat it as an idea rather than a fixed spot, and only try it if it is safe. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough. Then move in for a tighter shot of the carved reliefs.

The arch sits at a busy junction with cars, buses and trams, so watch the traffic and do not step into the road for a better angle. A second idea is to frame the view through the central opening, where a mountain, possibly the Serles, may fill the gap on a clear day.
text.geographic_location: The arch is at the southern end of Maria-Theresien-Straße, once the southern road out of the city. On its far side lies the Wilten district.
text.directions_text: Walk along Maria-Theresien-Straße to its southern end, where the arch stands. The phone icon on the map is at the arch itself, so there is no extra walk once you arrive. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the arch with the buildings around it. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or railings stop you stepping back. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved reliefs and to bring any distant mountains closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a wider frame with the arch in front, try the central traffic island at the southern end of the street. Treat it as a suggestion only. Do this only when traffic allows, and keep clear of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the arch centred, as it is symmetrical, with the vertical lines of the arch straight. Moving a few steps sideways can reduce street clutter such as signs and vehicles. For an alternative, step to the arch and frame the view through the central opening, where a mountain may fill the gap on a clear day. Check on the day which mountain appears behind or through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the stonework. If the sky is still too bright, try tapping on the sky instead and lifting the exposure slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, when the mountains are most likely to show behind the arch. Earlier or later in the day may mean fewer people and vehicles in the frame.

text.access_note: The arch stands in an open public street at a busy junction with traffic, so take care crossing; check the official Innsbruck tourism site before you go if you need up-to-date local information.

name: Innsbruck Cathedral
label: Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Domplatz' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Domplatz' (relation/1434544): middle (132 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/11550008: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cathedral of St. James' (76 m across).

text.description: Innsbruck Cathedral, also called the Cathedral of St James, is a Baroque church in the middle of the Old Town. Its two towers and big dome stand out among the green copper roofs, which makes it easy to spot and rewarding to photograph. The curved west façade is the part that works best on a phone. It is built of Hötting breccia and Hagau marble, and its niches hold limestone statues of Tyrolean saints made between 1941 and 1960. The present building went up between 1717 and 1724 on the site of a twelfth-century Romanesque church. The Asam brothers worked on the lavish interior. The church was badly damaged in an air raid in December 1944 and restored between 1946 and 1950. It became the cathedral of the Diocese of Innsbruck in 1964. For the outside view, stand on Domplatz, the square in front. It is the easiest place to get the whole façade and both towers in one clean shot, and the square and surrounding Old Town buildings in the frame show how big the cathedral is. Keep the phone level so the towers don't lean. Step back as far as the square allows, then take a second shot closer up of the statues in their niches. Warm, low light brings out the carved detail on the stonework.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the Old Town (Altstadt) of Innsbruck, on Domplatz, where its west façade faces the square. It rises above the green copper roofs of the surrounding old buildings.
text.directions_text: There is no tram or railway stop at this spot, so head for Innsbruck's Old Town (Altstadt), by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further out, and look for the twin towers. Once you are in the Old Town, the towers make it easy to find your way. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the square for a natural view of the façade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the towers will not fit, and use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the saints' statues in the niches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Domplatz. The cathedral's Baroque west façade and twin towers, framed from the square with the surrounding Old Town for scale. From there the cathedral's Baroque west façade and twin towers face you, and the square and the Old Town around it show the building's scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the towers up with the vertical lines so they stay straight. Include some of the square in the lower part of the frame to give a sense of size. If you are close, tilt the phone as little as you can, or use 0.5x from further back to avoid pointing it steeply upwards. Take one wide shot and one tighter zoomed shot of the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright part of the sky or stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the pale façade and sky keep their detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when warm light brings out the architectural detail of the façade.

text.access_note: The square outside is open public space, but the cathedral is a place of worship and photography inside may be restricted or need a small fee, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hungerburgbahn
label: Hungerburg Funicular
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hermann-Buhl-Platz' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hermann-Buhl Platz' (way/227387644): middle (53 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/359910: large area 'HBB: Altstadt => Hungerburg' (1762 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Hungerburgbahn is the funicular that carries visitors from the city centre up to the Hungerburg district, and it is as much a piece of architecture as a ride. Zaha Hadid designed the stations, and the current line opened on 1 December 2007, replacing an older railway that ran from 1906 to 2005. The line climbs 288 m in total. On the way it crosses the Inn on a 242 m S-shaped cable-stayed bridge with two pylons. The two cars have silver frames, with yellow compartments on one and blue on the other.

For photos, the best-known view is at the top. From Hermann-Buhl-Platz, the Hungerburg station's sweeping white canopy fills the foreground, and the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes rise behind it. This is the shot most often used to stand for the Nordkette lifts, and it works because the curved white shape stands out clearly against the mountain.

If you have time, you can add two more pictures. One is the slim steel bridge over the Inn, which makes a clean graphic line against the valley. The other is the concrete entrance and stairs of the lower station, a good opening image for the ride. Keep your phone steady and shoot the canopy as a simple, uncluttered shape. Snow can blow into the top station, which sometimes leads to partial closures after snowfall, so allow for that in winter.
text.geographic_location: The Hungerburgbahn runs from the Kongresshaus in Innsbruck's city centre, across the Inn and up to the Hungerburg district on the slope to the north.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Kongresshaus in the city centre, where the Hungerburgbahn begins, and ride the funicular up to Hungerburg station. Hermann-Buhl-Platz is the square right in front of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole canopy and the slopes behind it into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes above the roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Hermann-Buhl-Platz (in front of the Hungerburg top station). The station's sweeping white canopy in the foreground, with the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes rising behind it. From here the white canopy sits in the foreground and the Seegrube and Hafelekar slopes rise behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the canopy's long edge level, with the mountain slopes filling the upper part of the frame. Crouching a little can make the roof sweep more dramatically. If you also want a second picture, the steel cable bridge over the Inn works as a graphic line against the valley, and the lower station's concrete entrance and stairs make a good opening image for the ride.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bright white concrete to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the canopy keeps its detail instead of turning plain white. Check the edges of the picture for passers-by before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when direct light on the white concrete avoids the harsher glare of the afternoon.

text.access_note: The funicular and its stations are part of the public transport system and may be ticketed or partly closed in snow, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hofgarten, Innsbruck
label: Hofgarten
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/7745439: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hofgarten' (435 m across).
notes: Historic city park next to the palace.

text.description:
The Hofgarten is Innsbruck's court garden, a protected 10-hectare park on the edge of the Old Town, next to the Hofburg, the Kongresshaus and the Tyrolean State Theatre. It began in the sixteenth century on a river meadow, under Archduke Ferdinand II, and was then one of the most elaborate gardens north of the Alps. Over its long history it has been a Renaissance garden, a French formal garden and, since 1858, an English landscape garden. That last style is what you see today: wide lawns, mature trees and a set of ponds.

For photographs, the appeal is variety. You get tree-framed lawns, water, the palm house and the Tyrolean Art Pavilion in the middle of the park, which dates from 1733. Next to the pavilion are outsize chess boards, which make a friendly foreground for a people-and-place picture. Some plants were reportedly planted by Empress Maria Theresa herself, so look for the older trees.

Keep to the paths when you shoot, because walking on the ornate lawns is not permitted; only the sunbathing lawn by the children's playpark is meant for use. Take a few wide frames of the whole scene, then step closer for details such as the pavilion, a pond edge or the trunks of the older trees. Wipe your phone lens before you start, as park pictures look soft when there is a smudge on the glass.
text.geographic_location: The Hofgarten sits on the edge of Innsbruck's Altstadt (Old Town), beside the Hofburg, the Kongresshaus and the Tyrolean State Theatre.
text.directions_text: Head for the Altstadt and the Hofburg; the park lies right beside the palace, so you can walk in from the Old Town side. If you are coming from further out, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Hofgarten. From the phone icon on the map, the middle of the park is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 60 m south-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the open lawns and trees, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the pavilion and ponds. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details and for people at the chess boards, from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 60 m south-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the pavilion or a pond on one of the lower lines, with a mature tree trunk or branch at the edge of the frame. Keep the paths leading into the picture to draw the eye inwards. Hold the phone level so the trees do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its detail and the greens stay rich. Use portrait mode only for close-up pictures of people or a single plant.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light under the trees. On a still day the ponds may give you a reflection. Visit on a weekday morning if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The Hofgarten is a managed public park; stay on the paths, as walking on the ornate lawns is not permitted, and check the official site before you go for current access and palm house visiting times.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer under trees.
Ponds can give reflections on still days.
Weekday mornings are usually quieter than weekends.
The middle of the park is probably near the Tyrolean Art Pavilion, so looking north-east from the stand-here point shows lawns and trees.
The park can be entered from the Old Town side beside the Hofburg.

name: Helbling House
label: Helbling House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Herzog-Friedrich-Straße' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/747097019: the OpenStreetMap point 'Helbling House'.
notes: Rococo-decorated facade in the old town.

text.description:
Helbling House (Helblinghaus) is one of the most eye-catching façades in Innsbruck's Old Town, standing right across from the Golden Roof on Herzog-Friedrich-Straße. The building began in the fifteenth century as townhouses with an early Gothic look, and it was reworked in later centuries. The decoration you see today is frothy Rococo stucco from the early eighteenth century: bows, window frames, oriels, masks, sculptures and shells, all covering the front. The work was completed in 1732 by Anton Gigl. The house takes its name from Sebastian Helbling, who owned it from 1800 to 1827.

It photographs well because the façade is so full of detail, and because the raised stucco catches the light and gives the surface shape and shadow. Put the Golden Roof beside it and you get a picture that says Innsbruck at a glance. The best view is from the street directly opposite the house, on the side facing the Golden Roof, where the whole façade fits in one frame. The small square in front of the building also works well. For a second picture, step closer and fill the frame with the stucco angels, masks and flower ornaments. You can only look at the house from outside, so all the photography happens from the street.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town (Altstadt) of Innsbruck, at Herzog-Friedrich-Straße 10, directly across from the Golden Roof.
text.directions_text: Start from the Old Town (Altstadt) in the centre of Innsbruck and walk to Herzog-Friedrich-Straße. The house stands opposite the Golden Roof, which makes it easy to recognise. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full façade with the Golden Roof beside it. If the street is too narrow to fit it all, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the stucco details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, or from the opposite side of the street facing the Golden Roof, you can fit the full stucco façade of the house with the Golden Roof beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone upright, with the vertical lines of the façade parallel to the grid so the building doesn't lean. Place the house on one side of the frame and the Golden Roof on the other. For an alternative, move closer to the house and zoom in on the stucco angels, masks and floral ornaments.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the stucco detail doesn't wash out. Wipe your lens first, as it often gets smudged in a pocket.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when light falls across the façade so the stucco shows its shadows; a bright, even daylight also works well. Early morning is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The façade is viewed from the public street, but the house itself cannot be visited.

name: Tyrol Panorama Museum
label: Giant Panorama
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/45656980: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tirol Panorama' (87 m across).
notes: Museum with the giant Bergisel battle panorama.

text.description: The Tyrol Panorama Museum is at Bergisel, in the south of Innsbruck. It is best known as the home of the Giant Panorama Painting, which shows the Tyrolean Rebellion of 1809 on about 1,000 square metres of canvas. The painting was moved here in September 2010, and the museum opened on 12 March 2011. It is also linked underground to the Kaiserjäger Museum, and its exhibitions cover Tyrolean history and identity. For a phone photographer, the appeal is the setting: a large site in the south of Innsbruck, where you can photograph the building from a good distance back and add some sky. To photograph the building, you will need to step well back outside, a good distance from the entrance, to fit much of it in. Take a few frames at different distances: one wide shot to show the whole building, and one closer shot of the entrance or a detail. The inside of the museum is a separate matter, so ask staff about photography rules when you arrive. Opening times and entry details can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The museum is at Bergisel, in the south of Innsbruck. It stands on its own site rather than in the old town.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is given for this spot, so start from Innsbruck city centre and head south towards Bergisel. Local public transport (the IVB Sightseer, Lines 1 and 6, and the Stubai Valley Railway and Bus) is listed as serving the museum, so check the IVB timetable for the right stop. The phone icon on the map is at the centre of the museum's outline, so once you arrive, walk back outside the building to take your photos. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole museum will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance or signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step well back outside, a good distance from the building, so the museum fits in the frame, and keep to the public areas outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so it does not lean. Try one wide shot with plenty of sky, then a closer shot on the entrance or one section of the building. Keep other visitors small in the frame to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only when you really need it, as it can stretch the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the building, and fewer people. Check the museum's website for its current opening times.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening times and entry details.
